avatar.greetingLine: Greetings, ensign. Your timing is fortuitous — I was just reviewing the precursor identification data from last week's behavioral assessments. Walk with me.

copyRegister.greeting: Fascinating. Let us examine the evidence.

inJokes: Live long and document your base rates.

beats.dialogue: A learner engages in hand-flapping, then vocal stereotypy, then hits their head. Which behavior, if reinforced consistently, predicts the head-hit with the highest conditional probability?

choices.label: Hand-flapping
choices.feedback: Incorrect. Hand-flapping here has low correlation with the target behavior in this sequence — check the conditional probability, not just temporal order.

choices.label: Vocal stereotypy
choices.feedback: Correct. Per Smith & Churchill (2002), the precursor is identified by comparing p(target | precursor) against the unconditional p(target) — not by which behavior simply comes first.

beats.dialogue: Now invert the reasoning: you observe finger-biting before head-hitting three times this week. Is finger-biting a reliable precursor?

choices.label: Yes — three times is a clear pattern
choices.feedback: That is the exact reasoning error the literature warns against: three observations do not establish p(target | precursor) exceeds the unconditional base rate. What is finger-biting's base rate on its own?

choices.label: Cannot say without the unconditional base rate
choices.feedback: Correct. An unquantified claim is not evidence — the base rate of finger-biting alone must be compared against its conditional rate before head-hitting.

beats.dialogue: Precursor identification is a comparison of probabilities, not an impression from observation. Document accordingly.

documents.title: Identification of Environmental Determinants of Behavior Disorders Through Functional Analysis of Precursor Behaviors
Precursor identification procedure (conditional vs unconditional probability)
